Spec · 26 Slides

What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills

Each Slide shows its words as tabs above its Options, which are tabs too: open each, pick one, and dictate a note where it should change. Save at the bottom when done.

Brief

Format

Foundations, about 30 minutes.

Audience

Standalone for people who already use ChatGPT, Copilot or Claude at work, mostly tech-adjacent or non-technical, with no engineering background. They know prompting and chat, and want to stop re-explaining how they work and to know when a skill is worth writing. First shown right after participants used grill-me and to-spec; repeated and updated across workshops. Developers using coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) get the coding-agent view.

Style

Iceberg, with the control room of a research ship as the scene, drawn in low poly: its zones carry the title's waterline from what everyone sees down to what few look at, and a non-technical audience follows an expedition without any jargon.

Learning goal

Spot when a repeated task should become a skill, and tell what goes into the skill and what stays in project context.

Actionables

  • Pick one task you've explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill.
  • Write its description as the moment you'd need it.
  • Before sharing a skill, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner.

Hook

"You've explained this to the AI a hundred times. It has heard it once."

Red thread

Every conversation with AI starts from zero on how you work; once you've explained a task three times, a skill hands the AI your proven procedure on demand, and where you put the project details, inside the skill or beside it, decides how reusable it is.

Analogy

You are the captain of a coastal research expedition. The AI is your pilot of ten years, the best you know, with one settled condition: he forms no new memories overnight, but keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot. He steers an unmanned diving robot by cable from the control room on deck, and that robot is also the depth marker on the Iceberg ruler.

  • The expedition is the project context; one dive is one task.
  • A skill is a procedure card in the dive manual; its title and its "use when" and "not for" lines in the manual's index are the description.
  • Your standing orders in your own notebook are personal instructions; the expedition brief on the control-room wall is project instructions; the cable to the sonar and the lab database is a connector.
  • Shared skills go into the institute's fleet manual.
  • Revealed only on Slide 24: every pilot has the condition, pilot schools are the AI providers, a school's new course is a model update, and a pilot from another school is a different model.

The iceberg is the Episode's style, not a second analogy: each Section sits at its zone's depth.

Constraints

  • Two layers: the default view shows skills in a chat app, in its words (personal instructions, project instructions, connectors); an optional coding-agent view (Claude Code, Codex) has copy-pastable commands and the technical detail (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, SKILL.md, slash commands, MCP), switched per Slide to suit the workshop, like the views of the context window Explorable.
  • Not a law: keeping procedure apart from project context is shown as a design decision with trade-offs (performance, reusability, token cost), never as a rule.
  • Timeless roots: every principle in Sections 3 to 8 is cited from established engineering, information architecture or UX sources, not tool trends, and grounded once by "What works for people also works for AI", said as a strong rule of thumb, not a law.
  • Zones: A thought experiment and What a skill is at the Surface; When to write one and The label in the Sunlit zone; What goes inside and What stays beside in the Twilight zone; Sharing it at Midnight; Keeping it alive in the Abyss.
  • One scene: every Slide's picture is the ship's control room and its dives, except Slide 19, which shows the real grill-me files with the card only as a small key; Slide 5 sets the context window Explorable in the scene's words, and Slides 18 and 21 draw a matrix with small expedition pictures.
  • Low-poly figures with no detailed faces or hands; objects carry the motion.
  • The humour sits in the situation, never at the pilot's expense.

Research questions

  • Why do the established software engineering principles behind Sections 3 to 8 hold (the rule of three from Fowler's Refactoring, credited to Don Roberts, as a rule against premature abstraction; YAGNI and Knuth on premature optimisation; cohesion and coupling; Cunningham's technical debt; Lehman's laws), as each one's original source words it?
  • Why do the UX and information architecture principles behind Sections 3 to 8 hold (information scent from Xerox PARC; Hick's law; Rosenfeld and Morville's information architecture), as each one's original source words it?
  • Why do skills, personal instructions, project instructions and connectors load and get invoked the way they do across Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Gemini and Copilot, and what does each app call them?
  • Why do the agentskills.io standard and Anthropic's authoring guidance recommend writing skills the way they do (descriptions with "not for" lines, contents lists for long reference files, references one level deep)?
  • Why do skills help or hurt agent results, per Vercel's numbers (56% of skills left unused, a short AGENTS.md index beating discovered skills, a skill scoring below no skill) and any newer evals?
  • Why do organisations tier, own and review shared skills the way they do today, treating them like knowledge articles with an owner and a review date?
  • Why does a skill's audience and scope (personal or shared, general or project-specific) decide where its context lives and how much care it needs, and does any framework support such a matrix?
  • Why does "what works for people also works for AI" hold as a rule of thumb, and where does it break?
  • Why could people with amnesia like patient H.M. learn new movements without remembering the lessons, and how far does that picture hold for a model?

Style

Iceberg, with the control room of a research ship as the scene, drawn in low poly: its zones carry the title's waterline from what everyone sees down to what few look at, and a non-technical audience follows an expedition without any jargon.

Visual language

One scene throughout: the control room of a research ship and its dives, drawn flat in a 2D side view, low poly, no detailed faces or hands. The pilot runs the dives and forgets everything overnight; the captain hands over the work; the diving robot on its cable is the depth marker. A skill is the pilot's procedure card, the shelf of cards is the manual, and the dive order is the project context beside it. The iceberg is the frame, never a second analogy.

  • Zones. Surface: Sections 1–2. Sunlit: 3–4. Twilight: 5–6. Midnight: 7. Abyss: 8. Each section band and every Slide names its zone; a Slide never sets a colour of its own.
  • Zone grounds in the mocks are stand-ins. The zone tokens are built later, by implement-iceberg-style, and tuned by Han once they render; FE-011 bars palette colours. Until then the mocks show the light-to-dark ramp in neutral tokens: Surface bg-background, Sunlit bg-muted, Twilight bg-border, Midnight bg-muted-foreground, Abyss bg-foreground (text text-background on the last two). Build notes name the zone each ground stands for; the build swaps in that zone's shade of blue.
  • Depth ruler and rail. A section slide shows the whole ruler, one tile per Section on its zone band, plain zone label with the ocean term beneath; the view descends, rising bubbles pass, and the Section's tile lights. Every page Slide carries the slim rail at its left edge with that tile lit.
  • Motion. Descent once per Section; after that each Slide has at most one emphasis motion, shown in the mock at its end state. Nothing loops at rest; under reduced motion everything shows in its final state.
  • Colour. primary marks the one thing to look at (on Midnight and Abyss the focal mark inverts to bg-background). Meaning colours only for their meanings: pilot ai, captain human, robot and ship machinery machine.
  • Settled in the voice grill. Slide 2 offers at least a comic Option and a cutaway-illustration Option. The When to write one section slide carries the line "What works for people also works for AI". Slide 18's matrix is labelled "rule of thumb" in the drawing. Slide 21 is a callback zoom into Slide 18's matrix, reusing its drawing.
  • Art register, round 2. At Han's request the Title slide (with its section slides) and Slide 1 now show the low-poly art register: triangulated facets lit from the upper left, the iceberg cut by a glowing waterline, faceted sea zones in real blues, and the crew in large warm/cool planes, each with its one motion playing and a Replay control. Whether the other Slides follow is Han's pick in round 2.

Title slide and section slides

Each Option is a set: the Title slide, which sets the Hero motif, and under it the section slide of every Section, which echoes the motif and brings in its own Section. Picking an Option picks the set.

Section 1 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

A thought experiment

  1. You are the captain — Imagine you are the captain of a coastal research expedition. Your pilot has worked with you for ten years and is the best you know, and he steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck, while you decide where the expedition goes next.
  2. One settled condition — He has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. Stay the captain for the next few minutes, and hold on to that thought.
1

A pilot who forgets every morning

carries the Hook as a thought experiment, standing alone with no role switch: your best pilot of ten years forgets overnight, so you explain the same procedure every day; what would you do? Caption: "Every conversation with AI starts from zero on how you work."

Visual idea

master: grid-bento · motion: local

Caption: "Every conversation with AI starts from zero on how you work." A comic strip in low poly, the control room as the scene. First panel: a framed photo on the control-room wall, you and the pilot across ten years of expeditions. Then three mornings, each in its own panel: the pilot greets you with a speech bubble, "Nice to meet you", you explain the sediment sample again, and the robot sits idle on deck. The strip ends on "What would you do?" beside an empty procedure card. Panels appear one after another, nothing loops at rest, and under reduced motion all panels show at once. The Slide keeps only the question and the empty card, so it works without the live chat.

Voice script

  1. Three mornings — So tomorrow morning he greets you with "Nice to meet you". You explain how to take the sediment sample, step by step, and the robot waits on deck while you talk. The morning after, the same greeting and the same explanation, and by the third morning you could recite it in your sleep.
  2. The hook — That is what working with AI feels like today. You've explained this to the AI a hundred times. It has heard it once.
  3. What would you do — So here is my question, captain, and I would like your honest answer: if you were stuck with this pilot for a whole season, what would you do? If you're with me in a workshop, type it into the chat now. If you're watching the recording, pause here, look at that empty card and answer out loud. I'll come back to it.

Speaker notes

  1. Mollick's forgetful coworker — Ethan Mollick advises treating AI "like an infinitely patient new coworker who forgets everything you tell them each new conversation" [1]. Claude Code sessions each begin "with a fresh context window" and only written files carry knowledge across [2]. "Amnesiac" is the Episode's word, not Mollick's.
    • [1] Ethan Mollick, Getting started with AI: Good enough prompting, One Useful Thing (24 Nov 2024) — https://www.oneusefulthing.org/p/getting-started-with-ai-good-enough
    • [2] Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

The dive manual

sets the picture the Episode returns to: index entry, procedure card, expedition brief. Caption: "A skill hands the AI your proven procedure on demand."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x1 · motion: local

Caption: "A skill hands the AI your proven procedure on demand." One wide view of the control room: the pilot at the console, the manual open at its index, the expedition brief on the wall, and the robot on its cable through the window. Callouts name only index entry, procedure card and expedition brief. One card slides out of the manual on its own. The Spec offers Options for this Slide (comic, cutaway illustration), as Han expects a new kind of visual here.

Voice script

  1. The answer — Most people land on the same idea within a minute: write it down. Put the procedure on a card, keep the cards in a manual at the console, and he reads the right card each morning instead of you explaining it again. That is all a skill is, and the rest of this Episode is about doing it well.
  2. Three things to remember — Hold on to three things in this picture, because we return to them all the way down. The index entry is one line in the manual that tells him what a card is for, the procedure card is the card itself, and the expedition brief on the wall holds what is true for this expedition.
  3. The card slides out — Watch the card. He doesn't read the whole manual, one card comes out when the dive needs it, and (pause) that is the picture for everything that follows.

Speaker notes

  1. A skill spares you the repeat — Anthropic contrasts skills with prompts: a skill spares you from repeating the same guidance across conversations [1]. When a request matches a skill's description, Claude reads SKILL.md and only then does that content enter the context [1].
    • [1] Anthropic, Agent Skills overview — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview

Section 2 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

What a skill is

  1. Surface first — We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's look at what is actually on a card. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, there's a second view on some Slides that shows you the files behind each part.
  2. The mechanics, plainly — Even inside our story I want to be exact about how loading works, because everything later depends on it. So the labels beside the picture are plain, and they say what really happens, not what the story says.
3

A skill is a procedure card

defines a skill: a written procedure with a name, a description and optional files. Caption: "A skill is a written procedure with a name and a note on when to use it."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x1 · motion: none

Caption: "A skill is a written procedure with a name and a note on when to use it." One card in a clear sleeve. The front holds the title and the "use when" line, the back the numbered steps. Tucked into the sleeve are a species guide, a sample label and an arm preset. Coding-agent view: the same card beside its folder, each part linked to SKILL.md, references/, assets/ and scripts/.

Voice script

  1. Name and use-when — Look at the front of the card. There's a title, and under it one line saying when to use it. That line matters more than it looks, because it is the first thing the pilot sees and, as you'll see in a minute, often the only thing.
  2. Steps on the back — On the back are the numbered steps, the procedure itself. And tucked into the sleeve are the extras those steps can reach for: a species guide, a sample label, an arm preset. So a card is a procedure, plus the material that procedure needs.
  3. For developers — If you work with a coding agent, switch to the other view. The same card now sits beside a folder, and a line runs from each part of the card to the file behind it. If you don't, you can ignore that view completely.

Speaker notes

  1. What a skill is made of — a skill is a folder with a required SKILL.md (a name and a description, then the instructions) and optional scripts/, references/ and assets/ folders [1]. ChatGPT describes the same three parts in its own words: a name and description, workflow steps and supporting materials [2].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification
    • [2] OpenAI Academy, Skills — https://academy.openai.com/public/clubs/work-users-ynjqu/resources/skills
  2. Names differ by app — Claude, ChatGPT and Codex say "Skills", GitHub Copilot says "agent skills", and the Gemini app is replacing Gems with skills on 17 December 2026 [3]. Whether the Gemini app's skills are SKILL.md folders is not stated in the pages read; it is verified for Gemini CLI only [4].
    • [3] Google, About the transition from Gems to skills (Gemini Apps Help) — https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/18560919?hl=en
    • [4] Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/main/docs/cli/skills.md
  3. The "use when" line is the routing line — Google's Day 3 whitepaper calls the description "your routing algorithm" [5]. This is Google's framing of how a skill is chosen, not a measurement of how often it routes correctly.
    • [5] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills

Three levels of loading

progressive disclosure, stated as the mechanics are. Caption: "The AI reads only the index until a task needs more."

Visual idea

master: vertical-stepper · motion: local

Caption: "The AI reads only the index until a task needs more." The manual shown in three steps, each with a plain factual label: "Always loaded: every skill's name and description", "Loaded when the skill is used: its main instructions", "Loaded only if needed: references, templates and scripts". Under the third, a note that a script can run without its code entering the conversation, as Claude documents it. A soft light moves across the three steps in loading order. Invocation is not a level; it is the later Slide on two ways to call a skill.

Voice script

  1. Step one — Start at the first step and follow the light with me. This is level one, and the label reads: always loaded, every skill's name and description. So even with a hundred cards in the manual, all he carries around is the index.
  2. Step two — Now the light moves down to level two: loaded when the skill is used. Only when a task matches does he pull that card and read its main instructions, and not a moment before.
  3. Step three — Level three is the bottom step: loaded only if needed. Those are the extras in the sleeve, the ones he opens only when a step sends him there. Read the small note under this step, and I keep the exact claims in the notes beside this Slide, because they differ a little from app to app.

Speaker notes

  1. Three levels, stated by the standard — the Agent Skills standard names metadata (name and description, about 100 tokens) loaded at startup for all skills, the SKILL.md body when the skill is activated, and files in scripts/, references/ or assets/ only when required [1]. Anthropic states the same three levels [2]. Google's Day 3 whitepaper states them too: "1. Metadata (name + description) is always in the agent's context. 2. SKILL.md body is loaded only when the skill triggers. 3. Bundled resources are loaded strictly as needed" [6]. That is Google's description of the design, not a test that it works.
    • [1] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification
    • [2] Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview
    • [6] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
  2. Other apps load in stages too — Codex lists name, description and file path first and reads the full instructions when it decides to use a skill [3]; Gemini CLI documents metadata first, body on activation [4]. For apps whose pages were not read, the three-level claim is inferred from the shared format.
    • [3] OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) — https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills
    • [4] Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/main/docs/cli/skills.md
  3. Scripts: documented for Claude only — Claude runs scripts through bash and "only their output enters context" [5]. The other vendors' pages read say bundled scripts exist but do not say what that does to context, so keep this claim to Claude. Google's Day 3 whitepaper adds one line, that scripts "execute without ever polluting the token window" [7]; treat it as Google's statement, not as documented behaviour in other apps.
    • [5] Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview
    • [7] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
  4. What the index costs — Day 3 calls the metadata cost "tiny" but recurring: it is paid "on every turn" [8]. That is Google's claim; the size of the index comes from the standard's figure of about 100 tokens per skill in note 1, not from Day 3.
    • [8] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
5

Skills are dynamic context

callback to the context window: what's always loaded is static, and a skill arrives on demand, whether you call it at the start or the AI picks it mid-task. Caption: "What's always loaded is static; a skill loads on demand, so it is dynamic."

Visual idea

master: grid-2x1 · motion: local

Caption: "What's always loaded is static; a skill loads on demand, so it is dynamic." The context window Explorable with a Preset in the scene's words. Static, always there: your standing orders, the expedition brief and the manual's index. Dynamic, filling during the dive: the pulled card, camera frames, sonar readings and sample logs. Plain labels beside each: personal instructions, project instructions, skill index, skill body, tool results. The dynamic part fills as the dive goes on. A skill is dynamic whether you call it at the start or the pilot picks it mid-task.

Voice script

  1. Back to the window — Some of you have seen the context window Explorable, where we looked at everything the AI holds in its head at once. This is the same window, now in the words of our dive.
  2. The standing part — Start with what is always there before the dive begins: your standing orders in the notebook, the expedition brief on the wall and the manual's index. Those are static, so they are in the window whatever the task turns out to be.
  3. Filling as you dive — Then the dive begins and the window fills with the card he pulled, the camera frames, the sonar readings and the sample logs. That part is dynamic, and a skill belongs to it, whether you call the card at the start or he picks it halfway through. "Static" has exceptions, so take it as a rule of thumb, and the exceptions are in the notes.

Speaker notes

  1. Static and dynamic, as Google defines them — static context is always loaded: system instructions, rule files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md), global memory and persona definitions; dynamic context is loaded on demand: skill instructions triggered by task matching, tool results, retrieved documents and windowed session history [1]. This is Google's vendor framing of the vendors' own mechanics, not a measured result.
    • [1] Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-the-new-SDLC-with-vibe-coding
  2. Why Google separates them — Day 1 says static context "is expensive because every token is present in every interaction, regardless of relevance", and that too much of it "wastes tokens and dilutes signals" while too little "means the agent forgets critical rules" [2]. Day 3 repeats the split for the two files: "From one side AGENTS.md is always loaded within the project; Skills load on demand." [3]
    • [2] Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-the-new-SDLC-with-vibe-coding
    • [3] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
  3. "Static" is a rule of thumb — instructions are not strictly static. Claude Code .claude/rules/ files with paths load only when matching files open [4], Gemini CLI loads further GEMINI.md files just in time when a tool touches a directory [5], and Copilot path-specific instructions apply by file match [6]. By default, a skill's name and description are always loaded too, unless the skill is set to user-only invocation [7].
    • [4] Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project (Claude Code docs) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
    • [5] Google, Provide context with GEMINI.md files (Gemini CLI docs) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/main/docs/cli/gemini-md.md
    • [6] GitHub, Adding repository custom instructions for GitHub Copilot — https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/configure-custom-instructions/add-repository-instructions
    • [7] Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
6

Instructions, skills and connectors

tells apart rules that follow you everywhere, rules for one project, know-how on demand, and reach into other systems. Caption: "Instructions are always loaded, skills load on demand, and connectors reach into other systems."

Visual idea

master: three-column · motion: none

Caption: "Instructions are always loaded, skills load on demand, and connectors reach into other systems." Four things in the control room, each with its plain label and a small static or dynamic tag linking back to the Slide on dynamic context: your standing orders in your notebook (personal instructions, they travel to any ship), the expedition brief on the wall (project instructions), the manual at the console (skills), and the cable to the sonar and the lab database (a connector). Coding-agent view: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, SKILL.md and an MCP server. If the connector reads as too much in the render, the Slide falls back to three things.

Voice script

  1. Four things in the room — There are four things in this control room, and they do four different jobs. Your standing orders in your notebook, the expedition brief on the wall, the manual at the console, and the cable to the sonar and the lab database.
  2. Read the tags — Take them one at a time and read the small tag on each. Your notebook is static: whatever ship you board, those orders come with you. The wall is static too, but only for this expedition. The manual is dynamic, because a card arrives when it's needed, and the cable carries the sonar readings and the database into the window. That is the link back to the last Slide.
  3. Your words may differ — Your app may use different words for these four things, so match the picture, not the word. And if you work with a coding agent, the other view shows the files: the notebook, the wall and the manual each have one, and the cable is a server.

Speaker notes

  1. Instructions are always loaded, skills are not — Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md "at the start of every session" and loads a skill "on demand" [1]. Codex, Gemini CLI and GitHub Copilot document the same split for their instruction files and skills [2]. ChatGPT custom and project instructions were not read, and whether the Gemini app loads its instructions at the start of each session is unverified, so the split is not confirmed for those two apps.
    • [1] Anthropic, Extend Claude Code (Claude Code docs) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
    • [2] GitHub, Adding agent skills for GitHub Copilot CLI — https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-skills
  2. Names in chat apps — Claude calls them Instructions, project instructions and Connectors [3]; ChatGPT now says "apps (formerly connectors)" [4]; the Gemini app says "Instructions for Gemini" and "Connected Apps" [5].
    • [3] Anthropic, Understanding Claude's personalization features (Help Center) — https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features
    • [4] OpenAI Academy, Skills — https://academy.openai.com/public/clubs/work-users-ynjqu/resources/skills
    • [5] Google, Manage your tasks and workflows in Gemini Apps (Help) — https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/17094507?hl=en
  3. Connectors reach, skills know how — connectors are Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that add tools and data, not guidance [6]. Anthropic describes MCP as the connection and a skill as the knowledge of how to use it [7].
    • [6] GitHub, About Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Copilot docs) — https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/context/mcp
    • [7] Anthropic, Extend Claude Code (Claude Code docs) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
  4. Skill vs. AGENTS.md, as Google puts it — Day 3 has a "Skill vs. AGENTS.md" passage: "From one side AGENTS.md is always loaded within the project; Skills load on demand. The cleanest setups use both." It advises keeping AGENTS.md tight and, if needed, using it as a router into the skills library "with a short catalog at the bottom that tells the agent what's available" [8]. Day 1 calls always-loaded rule files static context [9]. Both are Google's vendor guidance on how to split the two, not evidence that the split works.
    • [8] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
    • [9] Osmani, Saboo and Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-the-new-SDLC-with-vibe-coding
7

Two ways to call a skill

invocation: you call it by name, or the AI picks it from its description. Caption: "You call a skill by name, or the AI picks it from its description."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "You call a skill by name, or the AI picks it from its description." The control room split in two. Left: you name the card, "Sediment sample, please." Right: the pilot scans the index and pulls the card when the dive needs it. Under the right half: "In Vercel's test of one Next.js docs skill, the agent never opened it in 56% of cases." Coding-agent view: on the left a typed command, /name in Claude Code and Copilot CLI, $name in Codex, @name in ChatGPT; on the right a description match. A highlight lands on one index line.

Voice script

  1. By name — There are two ways to bring a card into the dive. The first is the simple one: on the left you say its name, "Sediment sample, please", and he takes it out of the manual. No guessing involved.
  2. By description — On the right you say nothing. He scans the index while the dive runs and decides for himself that this task needs a card. His only clue is the line you wrote on it, so if the label is poor, the card stays in the manual, however good the steps are.
  3. Unused is real — Now read the line under the picture. It comes from one test of one kind of card, so I'd hold it loosely, but it should make you ask, in front of every card you write, whether the pilot would ever pull it.

Speaker notes

  1. Calling by name differs by app — Claude Code runs /skill-name at the start of a message [1]; Codex uses $ or /skills [2]; ChatGPT and the Gemini app use @ [3]; Copilot CLI uses a slash before the name [4]. "Slash command" is Claude Code and Copilot CLI wording; "by name" holds for all.
    • [1] Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
    • [2] OpenAI, Build skills (Codex docs) — https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills
    • [3] OpenAI Academy, Skills — https://academy.openai.com/public/clubs/work-users-ynjqu/resources/skills
    • [4] GitHub, Adding agent skills for GitHub Copilot CLI — https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/add-skills
  2. Picking by description — otherwise the model matches the task to the description. Gemini CLI adds a step: the model asks to activate a skill and the user consents before it is injected [5].
    • [5] Google, Agent Skills in Gemini CLI — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/main/docs/cli/skills.md
  3. What the 56% measures — "In 56% of eval cases, the skill was never invoked": the documentation skill in Vercel's default configuration for Next.js 16 APIs, not all skills in general [6]. Explicit instructions to use it raised invocation to 95% or more, and the pass rate from 53% to 79% [6]. In the default configuration the skill tied the no-skill baseline overall at 53% [6]. One vendor's eval, no named model, no replication, so treat it as an illustration.
    • [6] Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals — https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals
  4. Google's Day 3 restates Vercel, with two misreadings — it writes "a 56% non-invocation rate for skills expected to activate consistently" [7]. That turns one Next.js docs skill into skills in general, and calls Vercel's eval suite a "production analysis". It also says "a skill stripped of its instructions scored 58%, while the agent without the skill scored 63%" [7]. In Vercel's post that is the default skill against the baseline on the test sub-score alone, not a stripped skill, and overall pass rates were equal at 53% [8]. Vercel's own wording wins. Day 3 is Google's vendor guidance on how to use skills, not evidence that skills go unused.
    • [7] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
    • [8] Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals — https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals

Section 3 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

When to write one

  1. Sunlight — We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a card at all, and how to label it so the pilot actually picks it.
  2. Borrowed principles — From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law.
  3. Why a rule of thumb — It holds because the pilot acts only on what you hand him, like a newcomer on his first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.
8

The third time is the signal

when a skill is worth writing: the first time teaches you what's needed, the second refines it, and by the third you know what a good result looks like; the Section opens on "What works for people also works for AI", where the borrowed principles begin. Caption: "The third time, and you know what a good result looks like, is the signal."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x3 · motion: local

Caption: "The third time, and you know what a good result looks like, is the signal." A callback to the first Slide's comic, in three panels: explaining the sediment sample, refining it, then writing the card. The first Slide's empty card fills with steps. A small callout at the end: "Did you know? This matches the rule of three from Fowler's Refactoring", a software engineering rule against generalising too early.

Voice script

  1. Three tries — So when does a task become a card? Think about what you learn each time you explain it. The first time you find out what is needed at all, the second time you tighten it, and by the third time you can tell what a good result looks like, which is the moment you know what you would be writing down.
  2. Not only repetition — But counting is not enough. If you cannot check whether the result was good, you are not capturing a procedure, you are copying a habit, and the card will repeat your habit with great confidence.
  3. Did you know — Software engineers found this the same way, and I like that it is older than any AI tool. Look at the small callout: it is the rule of three from Fowler's Refactoring. I'll leave the exact wording in the notes, because the point here is only that people arrived at it the same way.

Speaker notes

  1. Fowler's wording of the rule of three — "The first time you do something, you just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplication thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor." [1] It is a heuristic, not a measured result. The credit to Don Roberts is in the 1999 book, which the research could not read.
    • [1] Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code (1997 slides) — https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2f09/a866bc7cb521227dc5ab2c4092096077c1ac.pdf
  2. Why treating the model like a newcomer works — Anthropic tells the writer to think of Claude as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows", and to show a prompt to a colleague with minimal context [2]. Anthropic Engineering calls building a skill "like putting together an onboarding guide for a new hire" [3].
    • [2] Anthropic, Prompting best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
    • [3] Anthropic Engineering, Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills — https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills
  3. Where the rule of thumb breaks — each is backed by a source, but listing them as the breaks is a synthesis: sessions start fresh, so only written files carry over [4]; rules in a file are "context, not enforced configuration" [4]; newer models read instructions more literally [5]; the same words read differently by model [5]; assistants drift toward agreeing with the user [6].
    • [4] Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
    • [5] OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide — https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide
    • [6] Sharma et al., Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548
9

Not every repeat deserves a card

YAGNI and premature optimisation: a skill written too early locks in an unproven procedure, and every quick skill is one more thing to maintain. Caption: "A card written too early locks in a procedure nobody has proven."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "A card written too early locks in a procedure nobody has proven." A manual stuffed with thin cards, several stamped "never tested". Beside it, a three-question check: does it repeat, does it have rules, does a mistake cost something? A small callout names YAGNI and Knuth on premature optimisation. The index grows line by line until it runs off the page, the one entry you need buried in the middle.

Voice script

  1. Too early — Now the opposite danger. If you write the card after the first run, you freeze a guess, and a procedure nobody has proven now sits in the manual with the authority of a card.
  2. A thin card has a price — Look at the manual on screen, stuffed with thin cards and several stamped "never tested". Every quick card is one more entry to keep right and one more line in the index, until the one you need is buried in the middle.
  3. Three questions — So before you write a card, ask three questions. Does the task repeat, does it have rules, and does a mistake cost something? If the answer is no to all three, leave it in the chat. This check is mine, a practical filter I use, not a published test.

Speaker notes

  1. Knuth on premature optimisation — "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%" [1]. His reason is a cost, and the same paper calls ignoring efficiency in the small "an overreaction", so it is a rule about timing and measurement. The quotes were not checked against the original (the ACM page returned 403).
    • [1] Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/356635.356640
  2. YAGNI, and what it does not cover — "Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them" [2]. Fowler counts four costs of a presumptive feature (build, delay, carry, repair) and says YAGNI does not apply to effort to make software easier to modify [3].
    • [2] Jeffries, You're NOT gonna need it! — https://ronjeffries.com/xprog/articles/practices/pracnotneed/
    • [3] Fowler, Yagni — https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Yagni.html
10

Write it from a good run

two ways to create one: from your own notes, or by letting the AI interview you about a run that worked, so the skill captures your intent, not only the steps. Caption: "Turn a run that worked into a skill: from your own notes, or by asking the AI to write it up."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Turn a run that worked into a skill: from your own notes, or by asking the AI to write it up." Two paths into one card. Left: your logbook pages from earlier dives. Right: today's dive went well, so before evening the pilot interviews you about it (why that depth, why that order, what would have counted as failure), then writes the card while he still knows. A callout: "Asking the AI to interview you works here too." Coding-agent view: asking the agent to turn this conversation into a skill. Both sources fold into one card.

Voice script

  1. Two starting points — Say it's the third time and you are ready to write. There are two good places to start: your own notes, like the logbook pages from earlier dives, or a run that has just gone well, today's dive, while it is fresh.
  2. Capture the why — With the fresh run, let the pilot interview you before you write anything: why that depth, why that order, what would have counted as failure. You want the card to hold your intent and not only the steps, because steps without the why break the first time the situation changes.
  3. While he still knows — Then write the card the same evening, in the same conversation, while he still knows how the dive went. Tomorrow morning he will have forgotten it, and that is the condition we started with. If you work with a coding agent, the other view shows the same move: ask the agent to turn this conversation into a skill.

Speaker notes

  1. Start from a real run — the standard advises: "Complete a real task in conversation with an agent, providing context, corrections, and preferences along the way. Then extract the reusable pattern into a skill." A skill an LLM writes from general knowledge alone yields "vague, generic procedures" [1].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices
  2. The agent can interview you — Anthropic's skill-creator checks the current conversation for a workflow the user wants to capture, extracts answers from it first, then interviews the user to fill gaps [2].
    • [2] Anthropic, skill-creator SKILL.md — https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md
  3. Google's route: run it without a skill first — Day 3 suggests asking your most experienced practitioner to "narrate three workflows they do regularly", picking the most repeated one, running the prompts without any skill loaded, and drafting a SKILL.md from the transcript. It closes with "Resist the urge to let an LLM generate fifty skills on day one." [3] This agrees with the standard's advice to extract from a real run. It is Google's vendor guidance, not a measured result.
    • [3] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills

Section 4 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

The label

  1. The label decides — We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A card nobody picks helps nobody, so the label matters more than the steps.
  2. Name, description — A label has two lines, the name and the description. That is all the index shows, and it is all he has to decide with.
11

The index is all the AI sees

at the start the AI sees only names and descriptions; information scent says the label must promise what's inside. Caption: "At the start the AI sees only each skill's name and description, so the label must promise what's inside."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "At the start the AI sees only each skill's name and description, so the label must promise what's inside." The manual from the pilot's view: the index readable, every card behind it closed and greyed out. Two entries side by side: a vague "Samples" and a clear "Take a sediment sample at a new site". A small callout names information scent, from Xerox PARC research. Coding-agent view: the name and description lines of a SKILL.md. The clear entry lights up as the dive's task appears.

Voice script

  1. The pilot's view — Sit in his chair for a second. The index is open in front of you and every card behind it is closed and greyed out, so you cannot peek inside. All you have is what is written on the label.
  2. Two entries — Look at two entries for the same card: "Samples", and "Take a sediment sample at a new site". A task comes in, because we've reached a new site. Which one would you pull?
  3. Scent — Researchers call this information scent, the cue on a label that tells you whether it leads where you want to go. So your job is to make the label smell like the task it serves.

Speaker notes

  1. Description carries the whole burden — because only name and description load at startup, "the description carries the entire burden of triggering. If the description doesn't convey when the skill is useful, the agent won't know to reach for it" [1].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/optimizing-descriptions
  2. Information scent — Pirolli and Card's abstract names "information scent models, which address the identification of information value from proximal cues" [2]. It is a finding about people foraging for information; that a vague label gives a model less to go on is an inference, not their finding. The page-646 definition was read second-hand.
    • [2] Pirolli and Card, Information Foraging (Psychological Review, 1999) — https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.106.4.643
12

Name the moment, not the content

describe when to use the skill, and when not to, in the words someone would actually say. Caption: "Describe when to use a skill, in the words someone would actually say."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Describe when to use a skill, in the words someone would actually say." Two index lines for the same card. The content label: "Sediment sampling procedure, steps 1 to 9". The moment label, in two halves: "Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed." and a closing "Not for water samples or filming." Above them, your request on the day: "Grab some mud here before we move on." Only the moment label matches it. A line is drawn from your request to the moment label.

Voice script

  1. Two labels — Here are two labels for the same card. The first names the content, "Sediment sampling procedure, steps 1 to 9", and the second names the moment, "Use when we reach a new site and need a sample from the seabed". One says what is inside, the other says when you need it, and that is your second step: write the description as the moment you'd need it.
  2. Your request — Now it is the day of the dive and you say, "Grab some mud here before we move on." Follow the line on the screen. Nothing in "steps 1 to 9" sounds like mud, but "a sample from the seabed" does, so write the label in the words you would actually say.
  3. The closing line — Last, the closing line of the moment label: "Not for water samples or filming." It tells the pilot where the card stops, so it doesn't turn up for a job it cannot do. Treat it as a choice and not a rule: the notes say who recommends it, and that nobody has measured it.

Speaker notes

  1. What and when — the standard says a description "Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it" and include keywords that help agents identify relevant tasks [1]. Anthropic adds specific triggers and contexts, because Claude chooses among potentially 100+ skills by it [2].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification
    • [2] Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices
  2. Write in the user's words — "Use imperative phrasing", "Focus on user intent, not implementation", and "Err on the side of being pushy. Explicitly list contexts where the skill applies" [3].
    • [3] Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/optimizing-descriptions
  3. The "not for" half is Google's advice alone — the standard and Anthropic recommend no "not for" clause in a description. Over-triggering is handled there by testing near-miss queries that share keywords but need something different, which "test whether the description is precise, not just broad" [4].
    • [4] Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/optimizing-descriptions
  4. Where the clause comes from — Google's Day 3 whitepaper writes "explicitly state what it is not for", gives the example "Do NOT use for employee shift scheduling or financial accounting", and its checklist says "Include when NOT to use to prevent over-triggering" [5]. It calls the description "your routing algorithm. It is the only thing the model sees to decide whether to load the Agent Skill" and asks to "be pushy if the model under-triggers". It gives no measurement that the clause helps, so it is Google's vendor guidance, a choice between sources.
    • [5] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
13

More cards, harder choice

overlapping labels compete, skills go unused, and a short index in the project instructions helps. Caption: "The more skills look alike, the less often the right one gets picked."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "The more skills look alike, the less often the right one gets picked." An index crowded with near-twins ("Sample", "Take sample", "Seabed sample v2") and a question mark over the console. The expedition brief on the wall carries a short list: "On this expedition, use these three cards." One callout names Hick's law as a finding about people; another gives Vercel's test, where a short index in AGENTS.md beat skills left to be found. The twins fade back and one line on the wall list lights up.

Voice script

  1. Near-twins — Now see what happens when the manual fills up. "Sample", "Take sample", "Seabed sample v2": three cards that sound alike, and a pilot at the console with a question mark over his head. He has to guess, and you made him do it.
  2. A short list on the wall — The fix is cheap. Write a short list in the expedition brief on the wall: "On this expedition, use these three cards." The wall is in view for the whole dive, so he doesn't have to decide from a crowded index. Watch the twins fade and one line on the list light up.
  3. Hick's law — Two callouts sit beside the picture, and I keep their details in the notes. What I want you to take from this Slide is the wall list: it is short, and it is always in view.

Speaker notes

  1. Hick and Hyman: a finding about people — Hick applied information theory to choice-reaction-time experiments with up to ten alternatives [1]. Hyman reports that reaction time rises linearly with the amount of information in the choice [2]. That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result.
    • [1] Hick, On the Rate of Gain of Information (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1952) — https://doi.org/10.1080/17470215208416600
    • [2] Hyman, Stimulus Information as a Determinant of Reaction Time (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1953) — https://doi.org/10.1037/h0056940
  2. The Vercel index — a compressed docs index of about 8KB in AGENTS.md reached a 100% pass rate against 53% for the skill by default. Vercel's working theory: no decision point, and skills load only when invoked [3]. It is a docs index for one framework, not a procedure.
    • [3] Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals — https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals
  3. Too broad, too narrow — the standard warns that skills "scoped too broadly become hard to activate precisely", while too narrow forces several to load [4]. No source measures lookalike skills lowering the pick rate directly.
    • [4] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices

Section 5 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

What goes inside

  1. Twilight — Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The card is written and labelled, and the question is what goes on it and what stays off.
  2. A decision, not a law — I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.
14

What goes where is information architecture

every piece of knowledge needs a home, and choosing it is information architecture; performance, reusability and token cost are said in the Voice script. Caption: "Where you put each piece of knowledge decides how well, how widely and how cheaply a skill works."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Where you put each piece of knowledge decides how well, how widely and how cheaply a skill works." One piece of knowledge, today's site depth, with two possible homes and their plain costs: inside the card, "always there, fits one site"; on the expedition brief, "fits every site, has to be looked up". The depth note moves from the card to the wall. A small callout: information architecture, the craft of organising information so it can be found.

Voice script

  1. A home for each fact — Take one piece of knowledge: today's site depth. It needs a home, and you have to pick one. Choosing where each piece lives is called information architecture, and you do it whether or not you name it.
  2. Three costs — A home costs you in three ways. Performance asks whether it will actually be read at the moment he needs it, reusability asks how many sites the card still fits, and token cost asks what it takes to load it into the window each time.
  3. Two homes — Look at the two homes on screen. Inside the card the depth is always there, but it fits one site. On the expedition brief it fits every site, but it has to be looked up. Neither is right in general, so it depends on how many sites you will dive.

Speaker notes

  1. Information architecture, in its authors' words — "a design discipline that is focused on making information findable and understandable" [1]; one of their four definitions is "The structural design of shared information environments" [2]. "The craft of organising information so it can be found" is a paraphrase, not their wording.
    • [1] Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., Part I introduction — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/information-architecture-4th/9781491913529/part01.html
    • [2] Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., ch. 2 — https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/information-architecture-4th/9781491913529/ch02.html
  2. Every line is a recurring cost — once loaded, a skill's content "stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost" [3], and every token "competes for the agent's attention" [4].
    • [3] Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
    • [4] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices
15

One card, one job

cohesion and coupling: a good skill does one thing and isn't tied to any one project. Caption: "A good skill does one job and isn't tied to any one project."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "A good skill does one job and isn't tied to any one project." Two halves. Left: an overstuffed card, "Sample, film, log and clean up". Right: a sampling card with "descend to 40 m" scribbled in for site 4; at the next site the seabed lies at 120 m and the robot hangs uselessly at 40. A callout names cohesion and coupling and gives Google's rule of thumb: "If you cannot describe what the skill does in one sentence, it is two skills." The robot stops short, far above the seabed.

Voice script

  1. Overstuffed — Start with the left half: one card that samples, films, logs and cleans up. Ask which job it is. When one card does four things you cannot label it, and he cannot pick it for any of them.
  2. Scribbled in — On the right is a sampling card with "descend to 40 metres" scribbled in for site 4. It was true at site 4. At site 7 the seabed lies at 120, and the robot hangs uselessly at 40 while he follows the card perfectly. (pause) The card was right and the dive was wrong.
  3. Cohesion and coupling — Engineers have two words for these two mistakes, and they are in the callout. Cohesion asks whether a card does one job, and coupling asks whether it is tied to one place. Look at the robot hanging at 40 metres: that is coupling.

Speaker notes

  1. Coupling and cohesion, as first written — "The fewer and simpler the connections between modules, the easier it is to understand each module without reference to other modules"; "Binding is the measure of the cohesiveness of a module", with functional binding the strongest [1].
    • [1] Stevens, Myers and Constantine, Structured design — https://doi.org/10.1147/sj.132.0115
  2. A coherent unit of work — the standard says a skill should "encapsulate a coherent unit of work that composes well with other skills"; too narrow forces several to load, too broad is hard to activate precisely [2]. The "if you can't describe it in one sentence, it is two skills" test is not in the standard; do not attribute it to it.
    • [2] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices
  3. The one-sentence test is Google's — Day 3 states it in its five rules: "One skill, one job. If you cannot describe what the skill does in one sentence, it is two skills. Decompose before writing." [3] This is Google's vendor guidance; the whitepaper gives no measurement that the test improves results.
    • [3] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
  4. Hard-coded details can override the task — in a benchmark of 98 public skills, a generic workflow template made the agent write files to .github/workflows/ when the task required ci/; the authors advise abstract guidance over templates with hard-coded paths [4]. It is one worked example, not a test of this picture.
    • [4] Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15401
16

Inside the card

domain knowledge can live inside a skill, apart from the steps until a step needs it. Caption: "Domain knowledge can live inside a skill, kept apart from the steps until a step needs it."

Visual idea

master: three-column · motion: local

Caption: "Domain knowledge can live inside a skill, kept apart from the steps until a step needs it." The card in its sleeve, each extra tied to the step that uses it: step 3, "lower the arm", points to the arm preset, which runs a fixed motion; step 4, "identify what you collected", points to the species guide, which opens on its own contents page; step 6, "label the sample", points to the label template. Two notes: when the steps get long, the next paragraph belongs in the sleeve; long extras start with a contents list, because the AI may only skim the start. Coding-agent view: SKILL.md linking one level deep into references/, assets/ and scripts/. Step 4 lights up and the species guide slides out.

Voice script

  1. Extras by step — So what can safely live inside? Domain knowledge, kept in the sleeve and tied to the step that needs it. Step three, lower the arm, points to the arm preset. Step four, identify what you collected, points to the species guide, and step six, label the sample, points to the label template.
  2. The long step — Look at the step that has grown long. When the steps swell, move the next paragraph into the sleeve and leave a pointer, so the card stays short enough to take in at a glance.
  3. Contents first — Now watch step four: the species guide slides out, and it opens on its contents page first. Do that with your own long extras too, so skimming the top is enough to know what else is inside.

Speaker notes

  1. Move detail into files, and say when to read them — "Keep your main SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files" [1]. The key is telling the agent when to load each file, for example "Read references/api-errors.md if the API returns a non-200 status code" [2].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification
    • [2] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices
  2. Contents list for long files — "For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top. This ensures Claude can see the full scope of available information even when previewing with partial reads" [3]. This is Anthropic's account of Claude's behaviour and no source measures its effect.
    • [3] Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices
  3. One level deep — Claude "might partially read files when they're referenced from other referenced files", using commands such as head -100, so references stay one level deep from SKILL.md [4]. The standard states the rule without the reason [5].
    • [4] Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices
    • [5] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification

Section 6 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

What stays beside

  1. Beside, not inside — Now the other home: details that stay outside the card, in files it reads when it runs. Inside goes the procedure, and beside goes whatever changes from one expedition to the next.
  2. Where it gets shared — Who uses the card decides how much care it needs. A card for your own use can be loose, and a card a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

project details can stay outside the skill, in files it reads when it runs. Caption: "Project details can stay beside the skill, in files it reads when it runs."

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

The card now says "descend to the depth in today's dive plan", and a line runs from that step to the expedition brief on the wall: "Site 4: 40 m. Site 7: 120 m." Coding-agent view: the step pointing to a project file such as CONTEXT.md. This time the robot reaches the seabed at 120 m.

Voice script

  1. The card points — Here is the mistake from before, fixed. The card no longer says 40 metres, it says "descend to the depth in today's dive plan", and a line runs from that step to the expedition brief on the wall: site 4, 40 metres, site 7, 120 metres.
  2. Same card, any site — Replay site 7. It is the same card with no edit, and this time the robot reaches the seabed at 120 metres. The procedure stayed put and the site details lived on the wall, which is your third step in miniature: decide where the project details live.
  3. For developers — In the coding-agent view the step points to a project file, say CONTEXT.md, and reads it when the step runs. For everyone else, the dive plan on the wall is the same thing.

Speaker notes

  1. Teach the class of problem, read the instance — a skill "should teach the agent how to approach a class of problems, not what to produce for a specific instance"; the example reads the schema from references/schema.yaml instead of writing joins into the skill [1]. Claude Code offers ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} so a skill can reference project files independent of where it is installed [2].
    • [1] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices

18

Who uses it, and where

the decision tool, as a rule of thumb that the governance Slide later expands. Caption: "Who uses a skill, and where, decides what goes inside it and how much care it needs."

Visual idea

master: grid-2x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Who uses a skill, and where, decides what goes inside it and how much care it needs." A simple 2x2, readable at rest and labelled "rule of thumb". Axes in organisational words: personal or shared, and general use or project-specific, with a small expedition picture in each square. Personal and project-specific: details written straight in, no upkeep. Personal and general: details kept beside, your own toolkit. Shared and project-specific: details can live in its extras, owned by the project team. Shared and general: details beside, with an owner, a version and evals. One card moves from your notebook to the fleet manual, losing its scribbled details and gaining an owner tag.

Voice script

  1. Two questions — Here is the decision tool, and it asks two questions. Who uses the card, only you or others too? And where, any project or one in particular?
  2. Four squares — Four squares come out of that. Personal and project-specific: write the details straight in, there is no upkeep. Personal and general: keep the details beside, it is your own toolkit. Shared and project-specific: the details can live in its extras, and the project team owns it. Shared and general: the details sit beside, with an owner, a version and evals. Watch one card travel from your notebook to the fleet manual, losing its scribbled details and gaining an owner tag.
  3. A rule of thumb — Read the label on the matrix: rule of thumb. That label is mine, and I mean it: this is how I think about it, so try it on your own cards and tell me where it breaks.

Speaker notes

  1. Where a skill is stored encodes who gets it — Claude Code skills in the home directory load "in every project", skills committed to a repository reach "everyone who works there", and plugins or managed settings reach "a whole team" [1]. Codex splits repository folders from user folders the same way [2].
    • [1] Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
    • [2] OpenAI, Build skills (Codex documentation) — https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills
  2. The matrix itself is an inference — no published framework combines the two axes into a 2x2 with care levels; the nearest are one-axis tier schemes [3]. Microsoft's zoned governance ties care to audience for agents, not skills: private personal agents, approved environments and admin approval for shared ones [4]. Label the square a rule of thumb.
    • [3] Saha and Hemanth, Skilldex: A Package Manager and Registry for Agent Skill Packages with Hierarchical Scope-Based Distribution — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16911
    • [4] Microsoft, Implement a zoned governance strategy (Copilot Studio) — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/guidance/sec-gov-phase2
  3. Why evals matter once shared — 40 of 98 skills change sign between two harnesses running the same model, so a skill is best evaluated "with the model, agent, and repositories in which it will be deployed" [5].
    • [5] Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15401
