How grill-me and grill-with-docs work

showcase of inside and beside together, on the real files, closing with one mention that a skill can run other skills. Caption: "The interview stays the same; what it learns about your project is written beside it for the next run."

Visual idea

master: three-column · motion: local

Caption: "The interview stays the same; what it learns about your project is written beside it for the next run." The only Slide outside the control room, a showcase on the real files. Three parts, left to right: the real SKILL.md of grill-me with the interview steps highlighted as the procedure; grill-with-docs, which uses grill-me and adds domain modelling; and the files it writes beside itself, GLOSSARY.md and decision records, with an arrow back to the next run reading them. A small key in the corner maps them to the card and the expedition brief. A closing line: a skill can also run other skills, with no settled name for it yet. GLOSSARY.md gains a new term after a session.

Voice script

  1. The interview is the card — Let me show you inside and beside together on real files, the only Slide outside the control room. This is the actual file of grill-me, a skill I use, and the highlighted steps are the interview, which is the procedure. It stays the same every time.
  2. Follow the arrow — Next to it is grill-with-docs, which uses grill-me and adds domain modelling. On the right are the files it writes beside itself, a glossary and decision records, and the arrow leads back to the next run, which reads them before it asks anything. The card stays the same, and what it learned about your project waits beside it.
  3. Skills can run skills — One last thing, in the corner: a skill can also run other skills. There is no settled name for that yet, and I'll leave it there.

Speaker notes

  1. Written beside, read next run — Anthropic says models, like people who use "file systems, inboxes, and bookmarks", do well with notes kept outside the context window [1], and a skill should teach an approach while reading instance details from files [2]. The grill-me and grill-with-docs files are this repository's own, not a research source.
    • [1] Anthropic Engineering, Effective context engineering for AI agents — https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
    • [2] Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices

Section 7 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

Sharing it

  1. Midnight — Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague reads your card?
  2. Three jobs — Three jobs wait down here. Give the card an owner and a version, decide who looks after the fleet manual, and test that the card actually helps.
20

Shared skills are knowledge articles

a shared skill needs what a company knowledge article needs; personal skills skip this until you share them. Caption: "A shared skill needs what any company knowledge article needs: an owner, a version and a review date."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "A shared skill needs what any company knowledge article needs: an owner, a version and a review date." Two copies of the same card. Left: your notebook card, with no header. Right: the same card in the institute's fleet manual, with a control block: owner, version 1.3, next review in March. A small note: personal skills skip this until you share them. The control block is stamped on as the card moves into the fleet manual.

Voice script

  1. Your notebook — On the left is your notebook card, and it has no header at all. That is fine while it is only yours, because you know who wrote it, when you last used it, and who fixes it when it breaks.
  2. Into the fleet manual — Now watch it move into the institute's fleet manual, where a control block is stamped on: an owner, a version, 1.3 here, and a review in March. It is the same card, now with what any company knowledge article has, and your personal cards can skip this until you share them.
  3. Why — Why bother? Because once it is shared, one author's edit changes what everyone's pilot does on their dives, and nobody knows whom to ask when one goes wrong. That is your third step: before you share a card, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner.

Speaker notes

  1. The registry entry — Anthropic's enterprise guidance says to keep a registry entry per skill with purpose, owner ("Team or individual responsible for maintenance"), version, dependencies and evaluation status including the last evaluation date [1].
    • [1] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise
  2. The review date is an adaptation — Knowledge-Centered Service does not review on a schedule: "Let reuse of Not Validated articles be the review" [2], and the page does not use the word "owner". Owner, version and a calendar review date combine KCS and Anthropic's guidance; no source defines them as a rule for skills.
    • [2] Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State — https://library.serviceinnovation.org/KCS/KCS_v6/KCS_v6_Practices_Guide/030/040/010/030
  3. The open format has no such fields — the Agent Skills format has no owner, version or review-date field; its optional metadata map holds them by convention [3]. Anthropic also says "Skill authors should not be their own reviewers" [4].
    • [3] Agent Skills, Specification — https://agentskills.io/specification
    • [4] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise
21

Who owns the fleet manual

governance, as a callback to Slide 18's matrix, honest that most organisations are still working it out. Caption: "Shared, general skills need rules for who adds, checks and removes them, and most organisations are still working those out."

Visual idea

master: grid-2x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Shared, general skills need rules for who adds, checks and removes them, and most organisations are still working those out." The earlier matrix returns and the view zooms into the shared, general square. Inside it, the fleet manual's front page lists what a card needs beyond the control block: who may add one, its tier (fleet, ship or expedition), its token cost, which robots it works with, and a retirement date. One corner stays dark and unlabelled, for the questions nobody has settled yet.

Voice script

  1. Back to the square — Remember the matrix? Come back to the shared, general square and zoom in. This is the kind of card the most people rely on, so it is where care matters most.
  2. What the front page needs — The front page of the fleet manual lists what a card needs beyond that control block: who may add one, which tier it sits in, fleet, ship or expedition, what it costs to load, which robots it works with, and when it retires. Each line is a question somebody has to answer before the card goes in.
  3. The dark corner — And then there is the corner we left dark, for questions nobody has settled yet. I want to be plain with you: I do not have the answers there, and I don't think many organisations do yet. If you have worked it out in yours, I would like to hear how.

Speaker notes

  1. Vendors tier by audience — Anthropic's tiers in claude.ai: personal skills, skills shared with individuals, group skills bundled in a plugin, and organisation-wide skills that only owners can add or remove [1]. "Fleet, ship, expedition" are the Episode's words, not vendor terms; vendors tier by audience and risk, not by how general the content is.
    • [1] Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization — https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13119606-provision-and-manage-skills-for-your-organization
  2. Who adds, checks and removes — the org library offers "Requires review", "Open" and "Off", a reviewer approves "a fixed version" and users stay on it until a new one is approved [2]. Anthropic says to pin production skills to a version and to deprecate skills whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired [3].
    • [2] Anthropic, Provision and manage skills for your organization — https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13119606-provision-and-manage-skills-for-your-organization
    • [3] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise
  3. Token cost and fit are per-card facts — a loaded skill is a recurring token cost [4], and a skill's value depends on the model and harness it runs in [5].
    • [4] Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
    • [5] Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15401
  4. "Still working it out" is a judgement — Anthropic's enterprise guidance lists what to track per skill (purpose, owner, version, evaluation status) and does not report how many organisations do so [6], so the unsettled corner is the Episode's judgement, not a measured claim.
    • [6] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise
22

Does the card make things better?

evals: run the same task with and without the skill, and test its label. Caption: "Test a skill by running the same task with and without it, because a bad skill can do worse than none."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Test a skill by running the same task with and without it, because a bad skill can do worse than none." Two test dives side by side in shallow water, the same task each time: on the left the pilot works without the card, on the right with it, each with a scorecard. Below, a small check for the label: a few requests that should pull the card and a few that should not, including near-misses. A callout: "In one benchmark, skills the AI wrote for itself scored below having no skill." The two scores fill in, one after the other.

Voice script

  1. Same task twice — How do you know a card helps? Run the same task twice in shallow water, once without the card and once with it, and compare the scorecards. Don't trust your feeling about it, because feeling useful and being useful are not the same thing.
  2. The callout — (pause) Read the callout for yourself, and take a moment with it. It is the reason the scorecard exists, and the details are in the notes.
  3. Test the label — Test the label too. Take a few requests that should pull the card and a few that should not, and be sure to include near-misses, the ones that sound like the card but need something else. Those show you whether the pilot reaches for it at the right moment.

Speaker notes

  1. Below no skill: SkillsBench, not Vercel — skills written by the agent itself land 8.1 to 11.5 points below the no-skill baseline on all three configurations tested [1]. In Vercel's eval the skill tied the baseline at 53%; only sub-scores dipped (lint 89% against 95%, test 58% against 63%) [2]. Do not attribute "below no skill" to Vercel's headline.
    • [1] Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12670
    • [2] Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals — https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals
  2. Bad skills can hurt, many do nothing — of 98 public skills, 92 showed no statistically significant effect, and harmful ones lost up to 17.0 points by anchoring the agent on their own templates [3]. Curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% [4].
    • [3] Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15401
    • [4] Li et al., SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12670
  3. Test the label too — the trigger set in the standard is "about 20 queries: 8-10 that should trigger and 8-10 that shouldn't", each run about 3 times [5]. Anthropic's guide says to build scenarios and compare against a no-skill baseline [6]. "Three and three" is in neither.
    • [5] Agent Skills, Optimizing skill descriptions — https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/optimizing-descriptions
    • [6] Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices
  4. Google sizes trigger tests differently, twice — Day 3 says a description must pass checks "to hit the industry-standard 90% trigger accuracy rate", the first being "You must write 3 positive and 3 negative triggers", with no source for the rate. Elsewhere it says "Write three eval cases (two positive, one negative) before drafting the body" [7]. Its own counts disagree, it is Google's vendor guidance, and none of it is measured.
    • [7] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
  5. Google's reading of Vercel is wrong on one figure — Day 3 says "a skill stripped of its instructions scored 58%, while the agent without the skill scored 63%" [7]. In Vercel's post that is the default skill against the baseline on the test sub-score alone, and overall they tied at 53% [8]. Vercel's wording wins, and SkillsBench in the first note, not Day 3, is the evidence for skills scoring below no skill.
    • [7] Singhal, Hernandez Larios, Dus, Nigam and Kolan, Agent Skills (Google whitepaper, Kaggle) — https://www.kaggle.com/whitepaper-agent-skills
    • [8] Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals — https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals

Section 8 · section slide, drawn in the Title-slide Options

Keeping it alive

  1. The Abyss — This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the card was quick, and keeping it right is the work.
  2. Nobody sees it — Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.
23

Every skill is a loan

technical debt: writing a skill is quick, and keeping it right costs something over time. Caption: "Writing a skill is quick; keeping it right costs you something every month."

Visual idea

master: vertical-stepper · motion: local

Caption: "Writing a skill is quick; keeping it right costs you something every month." One card with a running tag, like a loan statement, each entry a small cost that piles up: the site list changed, a new robot arm arrived, an index line now overlaps another card. A callout names Ward Cunningham's technical debt. The tag grows one line at a time.

Voice script

  1. Quick to write — A card takes five minutes to write. That is the loan: you get the speed now.
  2. A running tab — Then the statements arrive, one line at a time. The site list changed, a new robot arm arrived, and an index line now overlaps another card. None of them is a disaster, and each is a small cost that piles up. Engineers call it technical debt, Ward Cunningham's phrase, in the callout.
  3. Owning thirty — Writing thirty cards is easy. Owning thirty is the hard part, because the cost was never in writing the card, it is in keeping it right, month after month.

Speaker notes

  1. Cunningham's debt, in his words — "Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite." "Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt." [1] He names the failure mode as "the failure to consolidate". The software parallel to skills is an inference, not his claim.
    • [1] Cunningham, The WyCash Portfolio Management System — https://c2.com/doc/oopsla92.html
24

The pilot changes, the card doesn't

the late reveal of the analogy's world, and Lehman's laws: the world around a skill moves, so a skill that worked can drift. Caption: "A model update changes who reads your skill, so a card that worked yesterday can behave differently today."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "A model update changes who reads your skill, so a card that worked yesterday can behave differently today." A reveal panel: your pilot is not the only one, every pilot has this condition, and pilot schools train them, one school per AI provider. Two panels follow. Update: your pilot returns from his school's new course, same name and same card, but "descend slowly" now gives a different dive. Switch: a pilot from another school reads the same card in their own way. A callout names Lehman's laws, that software in use has to keep changing or it gets worse; here the world around the card moves. The same card goes into two dives that end at different depths.

Voice script

  1. Not the only pilot — Now I owe you something. I told you a story about a pilot, and here is where I let it open up. Your pilot is not the only one: every pilot has this condition, and pilots are trained at schools, one school per AI provider. You have been the captain of an AI the whole time.
  2. Update and switch — Two things can happen to your card. First the update: your pilot returns from his school's new course, with the same name and the same card, but "descend slowly" now gives a different dive. Second the switch: a pilot from another school reads the same card in their own way. Watch the same card go into two dives that end at different depths, because the card didn't change and the reader did. The callout names Lehman's laws.
  3. Hand over the verdict — So here is my question to you: which of your cards would you re-check after the next model update? If you own one, would you trust it to behave the same way tomorrow?

Speaker notes

  1. Lehman's first two laws, and their limits — "E-type systems must be continually adapted else they become progressively less satisfactory"; complexity increases "unless work is done to maintain or reduce it" [1]. The laws are disputed: only continuing change and continuing growth were validated by all studies reviewed [2], and Linux grew super-linearly [3].
    • [1] Lehman, Ramil and Wernick, Metrics and Laws of Software Evolution: The Nineties View — https://users.ece.utexas.edu/~perry/work/papers/feast1.pdf
    • [2] Herraiz, Rodriguez, Robles and Gonzalez-Barahona, The evolution of the laws of software evolution: a discussion based on a systematic literature review — https://doi.org/10.1145/2543581.2543595
    • [3] Godfrey and Tu, Evolution in Open Source Software: A Case Study — https://plg2.cs.uwaterloo.ca/~migod/papers/2000/icsm00.pdf
  2. The same words read differently by model — Anthropic's guide has model-specific sections on where "a single model behaves differently and what to change in your prompt" [4]; OpenAI notes that prompts optimized for other models "may not immediately work" [5].
    • [4] Anthropic, Prompting best practices — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
    • [5] OpenAI, GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide — https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide
  3. H.M. is an analogy, and it breaks at the card — H.M. learned mirror drawing and kept it across 3 days while remembering none of the sessions [6], because skills are stored by a memory system outside the damaged region [7]. For a model this maps only as analogy: trained weights fit the skill side, but a skill file is read as text, which makes it closer to a declarative note. That mapping is inference; Milner 1962 was read only through Squire's account.
    • [6] Squire, The Legacy of Patient H.M. for Neuroscience — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2649674/
    • [7] Squire, Conscious and Unconscious Memory Systems — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4355270/

Retire cards

delete skills nobody uses, so the right one stays easy to find. Caption: "Remove skills nobody uses, so the right one stays easy to find."

Visual idea

master: grid-1x2 · motion: local

Caption: "Remove skills nobody uses, so the right one stays easy to find." The fleet manual's index next to the season's dive log. Cards the log never mentions are greyed out and go into an archive box marked with their retirement date. The index left behind is short again, the one entry you need easy to spot, a callback to the earlier buried entry. The unused cards slide into the archive box and the index closes up.

Voice script

  1. Read the log — Last job: retire cards. Put the fleet manual's index next to the season's dive log and look at which cards the dives actually used.
  2. The archive box — The cards the log never mentions turn grey and slide into an archive box. Look at its date stamp: every card leaves with a retirement date.
  3. Short index again — And look at the index left behind: short again, with the one you need easy to spot. Remember the entry that was buried in the middle a few Slides ago? It is back in view.

Speaker notes

  1. Archive over delete — Knowledge-Centered Service prefers archiving to deleting, because deleting can break links and an archived article can be restored [1]. Anthropic says to deprecate a skill whose evaluations consistently fail or whose workflow is retired [2]. Reading the dive log to pick what to archive is the Episode's own method.
    • [1] Consortium for Service Innovation, KCS v6 Practices Guide, Technique 5.2: KCS Article State — https://library.serviceinnovation.org/KCS/KCS_v6/KCS_v6_Practices_Guide/030/040/010/030
    • [2] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise

The whole iceberg

lands the Learning goal and the Actionables with a peak-end close: a recap of the three steps, then the honest caveat that the deep end is still unsettled for most organisations. Caption: "Write a skill the third time, label it by the moment, and decide where the project details live before you share it."

Visual idea

master: horizontal-rail · motion: local

Caption: "Write a skill the third time, label it by the moment, and decide where the project details live before you share it." The full depth ruler from the Surface to the Abyss, each Section's takeaway written at its depth. The robot rises on its cable from the seabed to the ship, and on deck the manual lies open with a short index. Each takeaway lights up as the robot passes it.

Voice script

  1. Three steps — Let me bring the three steps up from the seabed. One: pick a task you have explained three times, and turn a good run of it into a skill. Two: write its description as the moment you would need it. Three: before you share it, decide where the project details live, and give it an owner.
  2. The honest caveat — I want to be honest about the deep end. Governance, review and retirement are the part I am least sure about, and I am still learning there too. If you find something that works, tell me.
  3. Your first card — The robot is back on deck and the manual lies open with a short index. If you want a low-key start, take the task you explained last week and turn its best run into your first card. Thank you.

Speaker notes

  1. What is settled, and what is not — no source defines owner and review date as a rule for skills, and none shows how many organisations govern shared skills at all [1]. The audience-by-scope matrix is a rule of thumb, not a published framework [2].
    • [1] Anthropic, Skills for enterprise — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/enterprise
    • [2] Saha and Hemanth, Skilldex: A Package Manager and Registry for Agent Skill Packages with Hierarchical Scope-Based Distribution — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16911
